newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry appeals for real tax reductions.
newsitem.headline: German industry appeals for real tax reductions.

text.p: As Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition met opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Thursday to discuss tax reform, German industry appealed to them to do their utmost to really reduce the tax burden.
The two sides were meeting in parliament's mediation committee, after the government's tax reform bill was passed by the lower house but rejected by the opposition-controlled upper house.

The German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT), Federation of German Industry (BDI), Federation of Employers' Associations (BDA) and the Federation of Skilled Craftsmen and Tradesmen (ZDH) warned both sides their decision was crucial to whether Germany would be competitive in future.

"From industry's point of view if the tax reform fails in parliamentary mediation it will have drastic consequences for companies' willingness to invest in Germany and will scare off foreign investors even more," the four groups said in a joint statement issued by the ZDH.
Coalition members appeared optimistic they would reach an acceptable deal on some points with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

Hans Peter Repnik, deputy parliamentary leader of the Christian Democrats and its Bavarian Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), told ARD television that in pre-mediation talks the sides had come close to a deal on company tax.
"I hope we will come a good bit further today," Repnik told German radio in an interview before the talks between Kohl's coalition of CDU/CSU and Free Democrats (FDP) and the SPD.

The lower house of parliament passed two bills last month aimed at cutting income tax by around 30 billion marks ($17 billion) over the next two years, but also including changes to corporate taxes that lead to higher burdens in 1998.
But last week the tax reform bills for 1998 and 1999 were defeated in the German upper house, where the opposition SPD, have the majority of seats.
